newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FOCUS - HUNGARY AGMIN SACKING HIGHLIGHTS DOWNTURN.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - HUNGARY AGMIN SACKING HIGHLIGHTS DOWNTURN.

text.p: The sacking of Hungarian agriculture minister Laszlo Lakos has underscored the setbacks suffered by Hungary's farm sector since communism collapsed.

From 1989 when Hungary scrapped communism, agricultural production has plummeted 30 to 40 percent as this agriculture dependent country lost former export markets in the east and failed to make sufficient inroads in the west, officials said.
"It's a very difficult situation," said one agricultural analyst, speaking on condition of anonymity.
"There is no driving force for agricultural sales because domestic consumption keeps going down.
"And the European Union (which Hungary hopes to join) is a saturated and very competitive market and it cannot substitute 100 percent."

Prime Minister Gyula Horn, in a statement by his office on Wednesday announcing the sacking, said, "A leadership change at the ministry has become necessary in light of the need for a national agricultural programme that would meet European Union requirements."
Lakos, speaking to Hungarian television, said the announcement had taken him by surprise but made no other comment.
Earlier, in an interview with Reuters before the announcement, Lakos said Hungarian agriculture showed some signs of recovery but admitted there were serious problems.
He said Hungary had been hit by bad weather, including three droughts in the past five years, which had severely affected some of the main crops.

This year, on the other hand, he said wheat production had been hurt by too much rain. The central statistical office in September said the harvest was down 14.8 percent from 1995, to 3.924 million tonnes, and down 36.9 percent on the average of years between 1986 and 1990.
Lakos said agricultural production could rise by as much as two percent this year, after creeping up 0.8 percent in 1995, but he said the sector was beset with enormous problems.
Among these is the privatisation of former state holdings, which has put small parcels in the hands of private owners, many of whom rent out the land.
"It is not the owners who are working the land but those who rent it," he said.

He said the government should provide financing so people farming the land could buy the parcels and said holdings should be rationalised so farmers could consolidate plots scattered in different locations.
"This is one of our biggest problems," he said. "We will need the participation of the owners."
Hungary also has had to focus attention on renegotiating an extremely unfavourable deal made in 1992 before it entered the World Trade Organisation (WTO), Lakos said.
Under the agreement, Hungary's export subsidies were cut to some 16 categories of foodstuffs from more than 700, and restrictive caps were placed on the subsidies, Lakos said.
"It is very bad...and it ruins our traditional trading basis," he said.
Hungary has since spent more on the export subsidies than the levels agreed with the WTO, provoking challenges from the United States and other major agricultural exporting nations.
Lakos said Hungary was reviewing a proposal from the United States and five other WTO member states resulting from a round of negotiations in Geneva in September, but he declined to divulge details.
